title: Judaism
paras: Judaism (romanized: Yahăḏūṯ) is an Abrahamic, monotheistic, ethnic religion that comprises the collective spiritual, cultural, and legal traditions of the Jewish people. Religious Jews regard Judaism as their means of observing the Mosaic covenant, which they believe was established between God and the Jewish people. The religion is considered one of the earliest monotheistic religions.

Judaism as a religion and culture is founded upon a diverse body of texts, traditions, theologies, and worldviews. Among Judaism's core texts are the Torah (lit. 'Teaching'), the Nevi'im ('Prophets'), and the Ketuvim ('Writings'), which together compose the Hebrew Bible. In Modern Hebrew, the Hebrew Bible is often referred to as the Tanakh (Tanaḵ)—an acronym of its constituent divisions—or the Miqra ('[that which is] called out'); it is sometimes also called the "Written Torah" ('Torah that is in writing') due to it being a closed canon of written texts.

While the Hebrew word Torah specifically refers to the Five Books of Moses, it can also be used as a general term for the entire body of rabbinic literature and any teachings based on those texts. This "Oral Torah" ('Torah by the mouth') includes both exegetical principles for textual interpretation and all rabbinic scholarship based on those principles. The Oral Torah comprises the Mishnah and the Talmud (collectively, the Gemara); the Tosefta; Midrashim ('Studies' or 'Expositions'); Halakha ('the Way'), or Jewish law; Aggadah ('Narrative'); and all subsequent rabbinic commentary and responsa.
